This page collects the PDF reports released by the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) in response to a Freedom of Information request for work by its Strategic Insight Unit (SIU). The requester shared the response bundle through [WhatDoTheyKnow](https://www.whatdotheyknow.com/request/research_by_the_strategic_insigh_2), following an ICO decision requiring the MPS to issue a fresh response.

The reports cover operational evaluations, research and analysis. The closest material to hotspot policing in the FOI bundle is the Town Centre Uplift Analysis. **The bundle does not include a direct evaluation of Operation Avert or Grip patrols.** Since it was released, however, the Home Office has published national Grip evaluations, and the MPS has published its Precision Stop & Search pilot evaluation. Those are separate public releases, linked below.

> **Release and handling note:** These files are copies from the FOI response bundle, not documents hosted by the MPS. Some retain labels such as “Internal to MPS only” or “Official Sensitive – Do not share”; those labels are reproduced as they appear in the released files. Check each document's own markings and context before reusing or circulating it.

## Place-based and operational evaluations

- [Town Centre Uplift Analysis (November 2022)](town-centre-uplift-analysis.pdf) — examines the effect of 19 Town Centre Teams across London. Finds a consistent increase in recorded drug offences across its two comparison approaches; results for other outcomes are mixed or small, and the report cautions against strong causal claims.
- [Precision Stop & Search pilot evaluation (26 February 2024)](precision-stop-search-pilot-evaluation.pdf) — evaluates a targeted stop-and-search pilot in nine wards in Lambeth and Barking & Dagenham, including training, community engagement, trust, crime and compliance strands. The report is marked “Internal to MPS only.” The MPS later published a public [Proof of concept evaluation (1 October 2025)](https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/met/about-us/research/precision-stop-and-search-pilot.pdf). London Assembly follow-ups record the publication, explain why the report omitted some drug-outcome breakdowns, and link to the MPS [Stop and Search Dashboard](https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/metropolitan.police.service/viz/MPSStopandSearchMonthlyReportv2/Coversheet) for some publicly available outcomes.

- [Operation Coniston short report (February 2024)](operation-coniston-short-report.pdf) — short version of a randomised trial of supervisor reviews of body-worn video from stop-and-search encounters. Covers search data, supervisor assessments and officer/supervisor views.
- [Knife Crime Prevention Orders impact evaluation (April 2023)](kcpo-impact-evaluation.pdf) — trial-based analysis of reoffending. Low uptake and few actual orders left too few observations for a confident causal estimate; the report finds no statistically significant difference in reoffending rates.
- [Positive Action workshop evaluation (May 2021)](positive-action-workshop-evaluation.pdf) — randomised evaluation of workshops for minority ethnic and female direct-entry detective candidates. The report finds increased assessment success among candidates offered the workshop, with larger reported gains for minority ethnic candidates.

## Other SIU research and analysis

- [Factors associated with strip-search in MPS custody suites](strip-search-factors.pdf) — statistical analysis of 403,208 arrests from 2019–2021, examining factors associated with custody strip-search, including offence type, location and ethnicity. The analysis is limited to strip-search after arrest.
- [Factors associated with missing-person high-risk grading (May 2023)](missing-person-risk-grading.pdf) — analyses how risk grades relate to contextual factors and subsequent harm, including differences by ethnicity.
- [Ethnic disproportionality at the point of internal misconduct allegation (November 2023)](misconduct-disproportionality-research.pdf) — mixed-methods research on possible drivers of disproportionality in the misconduct process. The report notes significant data limitations and is marked “Official Sensitive – Do not share.”
- [Misconduct research recommendations (November 2023)](misconduct-recommendations.pdf) — companion paper setting out high-level potential interventions and the need for further development and coordination.
- [Rapid Community Polling assessment: ZenCity](zencity-rapid-polling-assessment.pdf) — assesses the MPS trial of online community polling. The SIU reports problems with respondent retention and representativeness, and does not recommend renewing the ongoing “Blockwise” service in its current form.
- [ZenCity methodology report (April 2024)](zencity-methodology-report.pdf) — compares ZenCity polling with MOPAC’s Public Attitude Survey. Finds that the voluntary online sample is not a sound measure of London-wide trust and confidence trends.
- [Six ways to improve case-file quality (January 2021)](improving-case-file-quality.pdf) — qualitative research and descriptive analysis of barriers to good case files, with recommendations for supervisor feedback, review processes and targeted support.

## Original request and related records

- [WhatDoTheyKnow request: Research by the Strategic Insight Unit since 2021](https://www.whatdotheyknow.com/request/research_by_the_strategic_insigh_2) — request, correspondence and ICO-related updates.
- [MOPAC decision: Grip funding, PCD 1596](https://www.london.gov.uk/programmes-strategies/mayors-office-policing-and-crime-mopac/mopac-governance-and-decision-making/mopac-decisions/pcd-1596-ho-grip-funding) — funding decision and programme context, not an evaluation report.
- [MOPAC decision: Home Office Hotspot Response Fund, PCD 1650](https://www.london.gov.uk/programmes-strategies/mayors-office-policing-and-crime-mopac/mopac-governance-and-decision-making/mopac-decisions/pcd-1650-home-office-hotspot-response-fund) — funding decision covering hotspot patrols, problem-oriented policing and analytical support, not an outcome evaluation.
- [London Policing Board meeting record, February 2025](https://www.london.gov.uk/moderngovmb/mgAi.aspx?ID=38866) — records MPS discussion of its hotspot-policing randomised trial and subsequent evaluation work.

## Later public releases: Grip and hotspot policing

These are national Home Office evaluations of the Grip programme, not SIU reports and not an Operation Avert-specific standalone report. They provide the best published evidence I found on the programme's overall outcomes:

- [Evaluation of Grip and bespoke-funded hot spot policing, year ending March 2022 (published 15 February 2024)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hot-spot-policing-in-england-and-wales-year-ending-march-2022/evaluation-report-on-grip-and-bespoke-funded-hot-spot-policing) — national analysis estimated 7% fewer violence-against-the-person and robbery offences in hotspots on patrol days versus non-patrol days, equivalent to about 1,100 crimes prevented. Results were statistically significant at programme level, but only 2 or 3 of 19 force-level estimates were significant. The report says force approaches differed and treats them as separate evaluations.
- [Evaluation of Grip and bespoke-funded hot spot policing, year ending March 2023 (published 27 March 2025)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hot-spot-policing-in-england-and-wales-year-ending-march-2023/hot-spot-policing-in-england-and-wales-year-ending-march-2023-evaluation-of-grip-and-bespoke-funded-hot-spot-policing) — no statistically significant programme-level impact on violence and robbery volumes that year. It did find more positive crime outcomes on patrol days, including an 8.1% increase for violence and robbery. It also reported no evidence of displacement or diffusion in the available tests. This makes the picture less tidy than “hotspot patrols worked”: the 2022 aggregate crime reduction did not recur in 2023.
- [Home Office publication page for the 2022 evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hot-spot-policing-in-england-and-wales-year-ending-march-2022) and [2023 evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hot-spot-policing-in-england-and-wales-year-ending-march-2023) — source pages, with publication details and report text.
- [MOPAC decision: Home Office Grip Funding 2022–2025](https://www.london.gov.uk/media/103900/download) — describes separate MPS-funded work including Operation Nightingale, a randomised trial combining hotspot policing and problem-oriented policing, plus an Innovation Fund trial of static officer posts and drones. This documents funded trial plans, not their results.
- [Operation Avert conference presentation entry](https://anzsebpconference.com.au/6728) — identifies a 228-location crossover randomized trial and says the researchers presented results, but the public page is an abstract, not a full paper or report. I have not located a publicly downloadable full Operation Avert evaluation.

The key distinction: the Home Office Grip reports evaluate the programme across forces, using force-level evaluations and national synthesis. They are not a direct public release of the MPS’s Operation Avert RCT results. MOPAC records show further MPS trials were planned, but I have not found a public results document for Operation Nightingale either.

## Other later updates

- [London Policing Board paper: Disproportionality in Misconduct (May 2026)](https://www.london.gov.uk/moderngovmb/documents/s85317/6b%20-Disproportionality%20in%20Misconduct%20MAIN%20PAPER.pdf) — later public update to the SIU misconduct research. It reports implementation progress and further analysis, while noting the newer regression findings were awaiting peer review and impact evaluation was still to come.
- [London Policing Board papers, February 2025](https://www.london.gov.uk/moderngovmb/documents/g7178/Public%20reports%20pack%20Thursday%2027-Feb-2025%2010.00%20London%20Policing%20Board%20Performance%20and%20Finance%20Deliv.pdf?T=10) — state that the MPS had shared confidential findings from Operation Coniston and the Precision Stop & Search pilot with Board members. This is evidence of a later briefing, not an open report release.
